clinicalPearls: Characterised by inactivation of SMARCA4 (BRG1), a core ATPase subunit of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex, with corresponding loss of BRG1 expression by immunohistochemistry
Typically arises in the mediastinum, lung, pleura or chest wall as a large, rapidly growing compressive mass
Strongly associated with heavy tobacco smoking and occurs most often in middle-aged to older adults, with a marked male predominance
Morphology is undifferentiated or rhabdoid, with sheets of monotonous epithelioid cells and frequent necrosis
Immunophenotype often shows loss of BRG1 together with co-loss of SMARCA2 (BRM), variable weak or focal keratin, and expression of SALL4, CD34 or SOX2
Must be distinguished from SMARCA4-deficient non-small cell lung carcinoma, which retains more definite epithelial differentiation and glandular or squamous architecture
Diagnosis requires integrating morphology, loss of BRG1 staining and exclusion of other SWI/SNF-deficient and undifferentiated neoplasms
reference.pathophysiology: This tumour is defined by biallelic loss of function of SMARCA4, which encodes the BRG1 ATPase at the heart of the SWI/SNF chromatin-remodelling complex. Loss of BRG1 disrupts nucleosome positioning and the regulation of differentiation-associated genes, producing a highly undifferentiated, often rhabdoid phenotype. The strong link with tobacco exposure suggests a background of heavy mutational damage, and the resulting dependence on residual chromatin-remodelling and epigenetic pathways is being explored as a therapeutic vulnerability.
additionalDifferentials: Malignant rhabdoid tumour and SMARCB1-deficient neoplasms
Germ cell tumour of the mediastinum
Metastatic melanoma or large cell carcinoma
Ewing sarcoma and other round cell sarcomas
additionalInvestigations: Immunohistochemistry demonstrating loss of BRG1 (SMARCA4), frequently with co-loss of BRM (SMARCA2)
Panel to exclude mimics, including keratins, SALL4, CD34, SOX2, NUT and germ cell markers
Molecular sequencing to confirm SMARCA4 inactivation and exclude alternative drivers
Cross-sectional thoracic imaging to define the extent of mediastinal or pulmonary involvement
Staging imaging for distant metastases given the aggressive behaviour
Adequate biopsy sampling to allow the full ancillary panel in an undifferentiated tumour
redFlags: Large compressive mediastinal or thoracic mass in a heavy smoker
Rapid growth with airway, vascular or oesophageal compression
Poor performance status due to bulky intrathoracic tumour
reference.prognosis: The tumour behaves very aggressively, with rapid progression, frequent metastasis and short median survival despite chemotherapy and radiotherapy; complete resection is often not feasible because of extent at presentation, and immune checkpoint inhibition has shown responses in some patients, keeping treatment approaches under active investigation.
pitfalls: Confusing the tumour with SMARCA4-deficient lung carcinoma, which has different treatment implications
Assuming keratin negativity excludes an epithelial or carcinoma-related process
Failing to test for BRG1 loss in an undifferentiated thoracic mass
Misinterpreting co-loss of BRM as an unrelated finding rather than part of the characteristic profile
Overreliance on a single marker rather than the integrated morphological and immunohistochemical picture
references: WHO Classification of Tumours: Thoracic Tumours
WHO Classification of Tumours: Soft Tissue and Bone Tumours
management: Refer promptly to a thoracic oncology multidisciplinary team as soon as SMARCA4-UT is suspected or confirmed, given its rarity, aggressiveness, and overlap with mimics like SMARCA4-deficient NSCLC and NUT carcinoma

Complete surgical resection is preferred when the tumor is anatomically resectable and the patient can tolerate surgery, but this is feasible in only a minority given typically bulky, invasive presentation

Consider adjuvant systemic therapy and or radiotherapy after resection for high-risk features such as close or positive margins or large tumor size, extrapolating from management of other high-grade thoracic malignancies
For unresectable, locally advanced, or metastatic disease, platinum-based chemotherapy is the systemic backbone, often combined with radiotherapy for local control of the thoracic mass
Anticipate that responses to conventional cytotoxic chemotherapy tend to be limited and short-lived given the tumor's aggressive, undifferentiated biology

Immune checkpoint inhibition has produced responses in some patients and is a reasonable consideration when chemotherapy benefit is limited, though it remains investigational rather than an established standard of care
Use radiotherapy for local control of the thoracic mass, palliation of compressive symptoms (airway, vascular, or esophageal compression), and consolidation after systemic therapy
First-line treatment is platinum-based chemotherapy with radiotherapy added for local control where appropriate; there is no established standard regimen
For subsequent lines, consider immune checkpoint inhibition if disease progresses after first-line chemotherapy, given the limited durability of chemotherapy responses
Individualise treatment decisions beyond first line through multidisciplinary discussion and refer for clinical trial enrollment where possible, given the rarity of this entity
Stage and restage with cross-sectional thoracic and whole-body imaging to assess treatment response and detect metastatic spread
Monitor closely for local compressive complications (airway, vascular, esophageal) given the tumor's tendency for rapid growth and mass effect
Involve palliative and symptom-directed care early, in parallel with active anticancer treatment, given the short median survival typically reported for this entity
